articles.title: Buying Your Kid's First Phone Without The Regret | HeyPolo
articles.h1: Buying Your Kid's First Phone Without The Regret
articles.meta: Buying a kid’s first phone? See how to tell when they’re ready, how much you really need to spend, and what to set up before the phone reaches their hands.
articles.excerpt: The call came from a number I didn’t know. It was a woman from the dental surgery next to the bus stop, and my son was sitting in her waiting room, soaked, apologising to her. The bus hadn’t come. He’d stood at the stop for forty minutes in the rain, because he had no way to tell me, and by the time he gave up and walked into the first building with a light on, I was home wondering why he was late. He was fine, and she’d been kind. I spent the next evening reading about buying a kid’s first phone. Most of the regret parents describe later comes from handing over one device that does two very different jobs. It's a way to reach each other, and it's also an open door to feeds, algorythms, an expanding social life and a few hundred interruptions a day. Separate those two jobs and the decision gets a lot simpler. Keep them together and you'll spend the next two years negotiating with a rectangle. Readiness for a kids first phone shows up in behavior before birthdays Middle school usually forces the issue. Pickup times change, activities spread across the week, and suddenly your child spends forty minutes a day somewhere you aren’t, usually on a bus or on foot. If you’re still working out what age a child can walk to school alone, the phone question usually turns up at the same time. Pew Research Center reported in 2025 that 23% of U.S. parents of children 12 and under say their child has their own smartphone, and the share jumps to 57% among parents of 11- and 12-year-olds. By 11 or 12, more than half of parents have already said yes to their kid having a phone Age on its own tells you very little. The American Academy of Pediatrics reported in 2025 that a typical first phone in the U.S. arrives around 11, based on more than 10,500 children. articles.title: Why Scary Crash Stories Don’t Slow a Teen Down
articles.h1: Why Your Scary Car Crash Stories Won’t Slow Your Teen Down
articles.meta: Scary crash stories don’t slow your teen down. Learn what research says does cut crash risk for a new driver and what to put in place before their first solo drive.
articles.excerpt: You slide your phone across the kitchen counter with a local news story open on it. Two teenagers, a wet road, 11:40 pm. The unthinkable has happened. Your kid reads about 6 words of it, groans, and says “I know, Mom,” and goes back to scrolling. The research on why this tactic doesn't work is what stopped me from doing it. In its federal crash figures for 2024, NHTSA reports that drivers aged 15 to 20 made up 9% of all drivers involved in fatal crashes. Among those killed, 53% were unbelted. In other words, fear has had plenty of chances to work, but it doesn't. Seat belts and late-night driving have been the subject of staged wrecks in school parking lots for decades, and more than half of the young drivers who died still weren’t buckled. A teenager who is driving recklessly is, in their own head, invulnerable. A story about strangers on a highway doesn’t come into the equation when the chance to 'have some fun' comes up. What you can control is the set-up around the drive. That means teen driving rules the driver has actually agreed to, fewer teenagers in the car, and a way for the driver to see their own driving. The rest of this article covers how to do each of those. Your teenager already knows texting is dangerous In a Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and State Farm survey of more than 5,000 US students in grades nine through eleven, 79% said text messaging while driving is very dangerous. CDC's national Youth Risk Behavior Survey (2018) found that 39.2% of high school students who had driven in the past 30 days had texted or emailed behind the wheel. The 2019 cycle came in at nearly the same figure, 39.0%. Nothing in those numbers suggests an information shortage. Your kid knows. CDC also reports that among 2019 high school drivers, texting while driving was about as common among students earning mostly As or Bs as among students earning mostly Cs, Ds, or Fs. articles.title: Your Teen Is Learning to Drive From Watching You
articles.h1: Your Teen Is Learning to Drive From Watching You
articles.meta: Your teen is learning to drive from watching you, for 13 years before the permit. See what the research says about habits they copy, and what you can change now.
articles.excerpt: My daughter started calling out the yellow lights before her feet could reach the pedals. Years later I was the one in the passenger seat, on the way home from her aunt's house, and I watched her speed up for a yellow on the same stretch of road. I ever so slightly as she sped up a little farther away from the lights than I would have, but then it dawned on me - I knew exactly where she'd learned it. Your teen is learning to drive from watching you, and those lessons started long before they had a permit. Catherine McDonald of the Center for Injury Research and Prevention at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia put it plainly in 2020. "By the time a teenager gets a learner's permit,they probably have been watching their parents drive for 13 to 14 years." None of it was planned. It happened on school runs and grocery trips, stuck in traffic and running late. Most of us speed up for a yellow now and then, or take a call we shouldn't. That doesn't make you a bad driver or a bad parent. It does mean the most protective thing you can do before you hand over the keys is take an honest look at your own habits, and keep looking once the license arrives. Your teen is learning to drive from watching you long before the permit New drivers don't start from scratch. They start with ten years of watching you, and every new road gets measured against that. Then formal practice starts, and you're in the passenger seat. A Safe Kids Worldwide study in 2016 found that 84% of teens and 88% of parents said practice with parents made up the biggest part of learning to drive, and 75% of teens called it the most helpful part. So you're the example and the instructor, which is a lot of responsibility for someone who's also just trying to get to work on time. articles.title: Does Airplane Mode Turn Off Location Tracking?
articles.h1: Does Airplane Mode Turn Off Location Tracking
articles.meta: Does airplane mode turn off location tracking? It stops your phone sending data out, but the satellite receiver keeps working. See what actually changes, and what to switch off.
articles.excerpt: No. Airplane mode cuts everything your phone sends out wirelessly, which means calls, texts, mobile data and, by default, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The part that works out your position keeps going. Your phone can put itself on the map with zero bars, because satellite positioning never needed your carrier. It's accurate, too. Under the US government's standard for civil satellite positioning, good receivers have been achieving horizontal accuracy of 3 meters or better 95% of the time. Phones do worse indoors or between tall buildings, so treat three meters as the best case, and don't expect it in a parking garage. Even so, on a clear day your phone knows which side of the street you're on, airplane mode or not. Radios talk back, receivers only listen Your phone's cellular chip, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth all send as well as receive. They hold conversations with towers, routers and headphones, and those outgoing signals are what airplane mode switches off, so they can't interfere with the plane's radio equipment. GPS works the other way round. The receiver in your phone is like the FM radio in a car. It picks up signals that satellites broadcast whether anyone is listening or not, and it never sends anything back. There's nothing for airplane mode to switch off, so it leaves the receiver alone. What airplane mode does stop is the record your carrier keeps. The US Supreme Court showed how big that record gets in 2018, when it noted that wireless carriers had handed over 12,898 cell-site location points covering 127 days of one man's movements, roughly 101 points a day. That's a location point about every 15 minutes, all day, for four months. Each one was logged because his phone connected to a tower, which it does just by being switched on. Turn on airplane mode and those connections stop for as long as it stays on. That’s also why airplane mode saves so much battery.
